title: Sell Mineral Rights in Mountrail County, ND
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Mountrail County, ND
metaDescription: Mountrail County is where the modern Bakken boom started. If you inherited minerals near Parshall, Stanley, or New Town, get a straight offer here.
heroLead: The well that kicked off the modern Bakken boom was drilled in Mountrail County, and a lot of the families who own minerals here have been living with the consequences of that ever since, good and complicated both.
intro: EOG's Parshall #1-36H came in during the spring of 2006, and within a couple of years half the county had landmen knocking on doors offering leases nobody had seen the likes of before. Families who'd been ranching and farming the same quarter sections since the early 1900s suddenly had oil companies competing for their signature. Some signed fast, some held out, and a lot of the mineral interests from that era are still owned by the same families, just a generation or two removed and often scattered well outside North Dakota now.

We buy Bakken minerals across Mountrail County, from the Parshall and Sanish fields in the core to acreage further out toward Stanley, Palermo, and the Fort Berthold Reservation boundary near New Town. If you're holding a fractional interest you inherited and you're not sure what it's worth today, we'll tell you plainly before you agree to anything.

sections.heading: The Parshall and Sanish fields, still some of the best rock in the play
paragraphs: Parshall field and the adjacent Sanish field remain among the most productive acreage in the entire Bakken, which is part of why the discovery well here mattered so much. Operators have gone back through this ground repeatedly over the years, first with the original vertical-to-horizontal wells, then with longer laterals, then with infill wells targeting the Three Forks bench beneath the original Bakken producers.

That repeated development means a lot of Mountrail County spacing units now have three, four, or more wellbores draining them, which changes both what a mineral owner's royalty statement looks like and what a buyer is willing to pay for the interest. We check the actual well count and completion dates on your specific tract before we put a number in front of you, rather than default to the county average.

sections.heading: New Town and Fort Berthold trust ownership
paragraphs: New Town sits at the center of the Fort Berthold Reservation and a substantial share of Mountrail County minerals, particularly in the western part of the county, are trust interests owned by MHA Nation members and administered through the Bureau of Indian Affairs rather than the county recorder. Those sales move through a federal approval process, and we're upfront with owners about that timeline from the first conversation.

Fee minerals outside the reservation transfer through a standard North Dakota mineral deed recorded with the Mountrail County Recorder in Stanley. If you're not sure which category your interest falls into, send us your Division Order or an old lease and we can usually tell within a day.

sections.heading: Owners who moved away and never looked back
paragraphs: A large share of the calls we get about Mountrail County minerals come from people living in the Twin Cities, Seattle, Denver, or further away, whose grandparents or great-grandparents homesteaded around Stanley, Plaza, or White Earth and eventually left the ranch behind. The mineral interest stayed in the family because nobody thought it was worth the paperwork to deal with, right up until a royalty check or a lease offer arrived.

That's who we built this process for. We handle title research, Division Order review, and the deed paperwork by mail and phone, and you don't need to travel to North Dakota or hire local counsel just to get an honest look at what your fraction is worth.

sections.heading: What Bakken decline means for a Mountrail County royalty check
paragraphs: Wells in this county, especially the older Parshall and Sanish producers, are well past their peak production years now, which is normal for Bakken wells and doesn't mean the field is played out. It does mean the monthly check most owners see today is a fraction of what it was in the first two years after a well came online, and that curve is a big part of what determines a fair offer for your interest.

We also see Mountrail County statements with post-production deductions for gathering and gas processing that vary noticeably by operator, so two owners in the same section can have different net numbers even with the same gross production. Send us a recent statement and we'll explain what's actually driving your number before we talk about buying it.

faqs.question: Is my interest near Parshall still worth much this late in the field's life?
faqs.answer: Often yes. Parshall and Sanish are core acreage with a long production history and continued infill drilling, so mature wells still hold value, just priced against current decline and recent activity rather than 2008 boom-era numbers. We look at your specific wells before quoting.

faqs.question: My minerals are trust land near New Town. What's different about selling those?
faqs.answer: Trust minerals administered through the Bureau of Indian Affairs require federal approval to transfer, which adds time to the process compared to a standard fee mineral sale. We'll tell you honestly if your tract falls into this category and what the realistic timeline looks like.

faqs.question: I have a Division Order from an operator but never signed it. Do I still own the minerals?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, a Division Order just confirms your decimal interest for payment purposes and doesn't affect ownership. But an unsigned or outdated one is often a sign the title chain needs a closer look, which we're glad to do before any sale.

faqs.question: How do I find out how many wells are producing under my Mountrail County acreage?
faqs.answer: Send us the legal description from your deed or lease and we'll pull the state's well index and the Mountrail County recorder's records to identify every spacing unit and wellbore tied to your interest, at no cost to you.

faqs.question: I inherited a small fractional interest and don't think it's worth pursuing. Is that true?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Small fractions in Parshall or Sanish field can still carry real value because the underlying wells are strong producers, even if your individual share of the check looks small. It's worth having us look before you write it off.
